title: Modern C++ & Doing Things at Once

scenes.say: Two threads add one to a counter, two hundred thousand times in total. It can end short, and the total changes between runs. By the end, you'll explain why, fix it two ways, and read any modern C plus plus.
Interviewers expect modern C plus plus. Today you tour C plus plus eleven, then lambdas and templates. Then you break a counter with two threads, and fix it twice.
lines: Break a counter with two threads
Fix it with a mutex and an atomic

scenes.title: What type is auto?
scenes.statement: One C plus plus eleven word replaces a long type name. Work out which type the compiler picks, and what it silently drops.
scenes.say: A map's begin returns a mouthful of a type. For example, auto it equals m dot begin. Which type does auto pick?

scenes.head: Three drawers of new tools
scenes.say: Think of C plus plus eleven as a toolbox with five drawers. Drawer one makes code shorter: auto, lambdas, range for, null pointer. Drawer two is faster: move semantics hands over the guts, no copy. Drawer three is safer: smart pointers free their memory for you. Drawer four is constexpr: it runs a function at compile time. Drawer five is parallel: threads, mutexes, atomics.

scenes.head: auto reads the initializer
scenes.say: Auto copies the type from the initializer. Forty two is an int. Three point one four is a double. A string literal is const char pointer, not string. And the map iterator type writes itself. With no initializer, there's nothing to deduce.
Your turn. A vector of one, two, three. We loop with auto e, and double e inside. What does the vector hold afterwards? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `vector<int> v{1,2,3}; for (auto e : v) e *= 2;` v holds?

scenes.head: auto drops references
scenes.say: Still one, two, three. Plain auto copies. It drops references, and top level const. That's a const on the variable itself. Your doubling hits the copy. Write auto ampersand, and you double the elements themselves. Two, four, six.

scenes.title: Sort words by length
scenes.statement: Sort a list of words by length, with the comparison written right where you call sort.
scenes.say: Sort four words by length. For example, banana, fig, apple, kiwi. And write the rule inline, right where you call sort.

scenes.head: A lambda, taken apart
scenes.say: The square brackets are the capture list: outside variables it may use. Here, none. Then the parameters, like a normal function. Then the body. The result, sorted by length: fig, kiwi, apple, banana.

scenes.head: Snapshot or live link?
scenes.say: Now capture. We start with x equal to one. A by value capture copies x into the lambda, right now. A by reference capture keeps a link to x. Then x becomes two. The copy still says one. The link reads through, and sees two.
Your turn. A by value capture is read only. Add the word mutable, call the lambda three times. What is the outer c afterwards? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `auto inc = [c]() mutable { return ++c; };` After 3 calls, outer `c`?

scenes.head: mutable changes only the copy
scenes.say: Zero. Mutable lets the lambda change its own copy, and it remembers that copy between calls. So three calls return three. But the outer c never moved. By value capture is read only without mutable, because the call operator is const.

scenes.head: The trap: a dangling capture
scenes.say: The classic trap. This lambda captures a local by reference, and leaves the function. When make returns, local dies, and the lambda holds a dangling reference. Calling it is undefined. Under the hood, a lambda is just a hidden class, and captures are members. If it outlives the scope, capture by value.

scenes.title: One max for every type
scenes.statement: Write max once, so it works for int, double and string.
scenes.say: One max function, any type. For example, three and seven. Or two point five and one point five. Write it once.

scenes.head: T is a placeholder type
scenes.say: Without templates, we'd write max for int, again for double, again for string. With one, T is a placeholder. Two ints: T is int. Two doubles: T is double. Or spell it in angle brackets, for string.
Your turn. Same maxOf. We call it with the int three and the double two point five. What happens? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: A recipe, stamped per type
scenes.say: Compile error: T can't be both. A template is a recipe, not code. Each use makes the compiler stamp a real function, for int, for double. All at compile time, so no runtime cost, only longer builds.

scenes.head: Full specialization
scenes.say: Specialization swaps in a different version for specific types. First the primary template, which returns unknown. Then template, empty angle brackets, and the exact type: int. TypeName of int prints int. Double has no special version, so it falls back to unknown.

scenes.head: Why: generic can be wrong
scenes.say: Why bother? Generic equality uses double equals. For C strings, that compares addresses, not text. So specialize for const char pointer, and call strcmp. Partial specialization matches a whole family: T star is any pointer. Classes only. Functions overload instead.

scenes.title: Why does the counter lose adds?
scenes.statement: Two threads each add one to a shared counter, one hundred thousand times. We expect two hundred thousand.
scenes.say: Now for the bug in the hook. Two threads, one counter. For example, a hundred thousand adds each. We expect two hundred thousand. One run printed one hundred twenty two thousand, forty two.

scenes.head: One increment is three steps
scenes.say: Plus plus looks like one step. It's three: read, add, write. Counter is five. Thread A reads five. Thread B reads five, too. A writes six. B writes six. Two adds, one result. One increment is lost.

scenes.head: That is a data race
scenes.say: This is the code. Both threads write the same int, with no lock. That's a data race, and in C plus plus it's undefined behavior. A race condition is broader: any timing bug, even with atomics. Run it a few times with optimization off, and the total can come up short and change between runs. With optimization on, it may still print two hundred thousand. The bug is still there.

panels.label: g++ -O0

steps.cue: the total can come up short

scenes.say: Your turn. Four fixes, and only one actually works. Which one? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Which fix makes `++counter` safe across two threads?

scenes.head: Fix one: an atomic counter
scenes.say: Atomic is the right answer for one counter. Volatile is not atomic, and sleep only changes timing. Atomic makes plus plus one indivisible step, with no lock. Each thread adds its hundred thousand. The total is two hundred thousand, every time. A mutex also works, and the next scene shows how to lock it.

scenes.head: Why lock_guard, not lock()
scenes.say: Why not call lock and unlock yourself? Every path out must unlock. An early return skips it. If process throws, it's skipped too, and the next thread hangs forever. Lock guard is tiny. Its constructor locks, its destructor unlocks, so every exit unlocks. That's R A I I, resource acquisition is initialization. The guard releases the lock when it leaves scope.

panels.label: manual
lock_guard

scenes.head: atomic versus mutex
scenes.say: An atomic protects one variable, usually with no lock. A mutex protects any block. Atomics use C P U instructions. Mutexes can block and sleep. Atomics are cheaper for simple updates. For counters and flags, atomic. For several values that change together, a mutex.
rows: C P U instruction, usually no lock

scenes.title: Run it, and get the answer
scenes.statement: Run compute on another thread, and get its result back, or its exception. Which tool fits?
scenes.say: How do you get an answer back from another thread? For example, compute returns forty two. We want the answer. Which tool?

scenes.head: std::thread: you manage it
scenes.say: S t d thread starts immediately. It has no return value, so we write into a shared variable. You must join or detach before the thread object dies. An exception escaping the thread function also aborts the program. It's a low level tool.
Your turn. We create a thread, and let the object go out of scope without join or detach. What happens? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: A joinable `thread` is destroyed without `join()`. Result?

scenes.head: std::async: a task with a future
scenes.say: Program aborts. We call that terminate. A joinable thread's destructor does that. That's why async exists. It runs the function and hands back a future. Get waits, then returns the value, or rethrows compute's exception, here, in your thread. With launch async it runs on a new thread. With the default policy, it may run lazily inside get.

scenes.head: thread versus async
scenes.say: A thread is low level. Async is a task. Results: none, against a future. Exceptions: a thread terminates, async stores them for get. Cleanup: join or detach, against the future waiting. Start: immediately, against by launch policy. Long lived workers: thread. Just an answer: async.
rows: compute this, give me the answer

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What did C plus plus eleven add? Syntax: auto, lambdas, range for, null pointer. Performance and safety: move semantics, smart pointers, constexpr. And threads, mutexes and atomics.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What does auto do? It deduces the type from the initializer, at compile time. It drops references and top level const, so write auto ampersand to avoid copies.
rows: type deduced from the initializer, at compile time

scenes.say: Auto deduces the type from the initializer, at compile time. It drops references, so write auto ampersand to avoid copies.
lines: Drops & and const: write auto& to copy less

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is a lambda? An unnamed function object written inline. The compiler makes a class with a call operator, and captures become members. Use it for algorithms, callbacks, threads.
rows: a class with `operator()`; captures are members

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Capture by value versus reference? Value copies when the lambda is created. Reference links to the live variable. Value is read only unless mutable. If the lambda outlives the scope, capture by value.
rows: reference dangles if it outlives the scope

scenes.say: A lambda is a class with a call operator. Capture by value copies. Capture by reference links. If it outlives the scope, capture by value.
lines: By value copies; by reference links

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What are templates? Code parameterized by type, written once. The compiler instantiates a version per type, at compile time. No runtime cost, but longer builds. Usually in headers.
rows: code parameterized by type, written once
one instantiation per type, at compile time

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Template specialization? A custom version for specific types. Full: template, empty brackets, one exact type. Partial: a pattern like T star, classes only. Used for type traits and when generic code is wrong.
rows: a custom implementation for specific types
full: one exact type; partial: a pattern, classes only
traits, or generic code is wrong, like `const char*`

scenes.say: A template is one recipe, stamped per type, at compile time. Specialization gives one type its own version.
lines: Template: one recipe, stamped per type
Specialization: a custom version for one type

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Thread versus async? A thread starts now, returns nothing, and must be joined. Async returns a future, and get brings the value or the exception. Use launch async to force a new thread.
rows: starts now, no result, join or detach
runs a task, returns a future

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Race condition? The result depends on thread timing. A data race: unsynchronized shared access with a writer, undefined behavior. Fix with a mutex or atomic, and make check then act one step.
rows: unsynchronized shared access, one writer: UB
mutex or atomic; check-then-act in one step

scenes.say: Remember the pair. Thread starts now, returns nothing, and needs a join. Async returns a future. A race needs unsynchronized writes. Fix it with a mutex or an atomic.
lines: Thread: starts now, no result, must join
Async: a future, get brings the value
Race: unsynchronized writes; use a mutex

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Mutex and lock guard? A mutex is a lock only one thread holds. Lock guard locks in its constructor, unlocks in its destructor. Returns and exceptions release it. Keep the locked scope small.
rows: a lock only one thread can hold
RAII: lock in constructor, unlock in destructor

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Atomic versus mutex? Atomic: one variable, one operation, usually lock free. Mutex: a whole region, others block. A counter or flag: atomic. Several values together: mutex.
rows: counter or flag: atomic; several values: mutex

scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode eleven fourteen, Print in Order, is thread ordering. LeetCode eleven fifteen, Print FooBar Alternately, makes two threads take turns. LeetCode eleven sixteen, Print Zero Even Odd, coordinates three threads.

scenes.say: So say this. Auto and lambdas copy by default. Plus plus is three steps, so two threads lose adds. Write the ampersand on purpose. Fix it with an atomic for one variable, or a lock guard for a block.
